phy_ocra.14.0.summary: An atom is made of a tiny, dense, **positively charged nucleus** containing protons and neutrons, surrounded by **negatively charged electrons**. The nucleus is about 100 000 times smaller in radius than the atom, yet contains almost all of its mass. Every element has a fixed number of protons (its **atomic number**), but atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons: these are **isotopes**. Nuclear notation, written as the mass number above the atomic number beside the element symbol, lets you work out the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons and compare isotopes.

core.p: Every atom has a **nucleus** at its centre containing **protons** and **neutrons**. **Electrons** move around the nucleus in **energy levels (shells)**. The nucleus is **positively charged** because protons are positive and neutrons are neutral.
bullets: **Protons**: in the nucleus, charge **+1**, relative mass **1**.
**Neutrons**: in the nucleus, charge **0** (neutral), relative mass **1**.
**Electrons**: in shells around the nucleus, charge **-1**, relative mass about **1/2000** (very small).
Protons and neutrons are together called **nucleons**.
Almost all of the **mass** of the atom is in the nucleus.

callouts.p: The particle table is worth easy marks: location, relative charge and relative mass of protons, neutrons and electrons.

core.h: Size of the atom and the nucleus
core.p: Atoms are extremely small, and the nucleus is tiny even compared with the atom. OCR expects you to recall typical sizes as **orders of magnitude**.
bullets: Radius of an atom is about **1 x 10^-10 m** (0.1 nm).
Radius of a nucleus is about **1 x 10^-15 m**.
So the nucleus radius is about **100 000 (10^5) times smaller** than the atom.
Small molecules are of the order of **10^-10 m** too.
Most of the atom is therefore **empty space**.
Even though it is tiny, the nucleus contains **almost all the mass**, so it is extremely **dense**.

callouts.p: Atom about 10^-10 m, nucleus about 10^-15 m: the atom is about 100 000 times wider than its nucleus.
If the nucleus were a marble on the centre spot, the atom would be the size of a football stadium.

core.p: An atom has **equal numbers of protons and electrons**, so the positive and negative charges cancel and the atom is **neutral overall**. The nucleus itself is positive.
bullets: Number of electrons = number of protons in a **neutral atom**.
The charge on the nucleus = **+(number of protons)** in units of the proton charge.
Each element's nucleus has a **characteristic positive charge** because each element has its own number of protons.
If an atom **loses** electrons it becomes a **positive ion**; if it **gains** electrons it becomes a **negative ion**.
Changing the number of electrons does **not** change the element; changing the number of protons does.

callouts.p: The atom is neutral, but the nucleus is positive. Do not confuse them.

core.h: How the model of the atom developed
core.p: Scientists changed the model of the atom as new **experimental evidence** appeared. A model is replaced when it cannot explain new observations.
bullets: **Dalton (early 1800s)**: atoms are tiny solid spheres that cannot be divided.
**Thomson (1897)**: discovered the **electron**; proposed the **plum pudding model**, a ball of positive charge with electrons embedded in it.
**Rutherford, Geiger and Marsden (1909 to 1911)**: **alpha particle scattering experiment** showed a tiny, dense, positive **nucleus** with mostly empty space around it.
**Bohr (1913)**: electrons orbit the nucleus in fixed **energy levels (shells)**.
**Chadwick (1932)**: discovered the **neutron** in the nucleus, explaining why nuclear masses were larger than the protons alone could explain.

Model or discovery

callouts.p: A new model is accepted when new experimental evidence cannot be explained by the old one and the new model explains it.

core.p: Rutherford's team fired **alpha particles** (positive) at a very thin **gold foil**. The results disproved the plum pudding model.
bullets: **Most alpha particles passed straight through**: the atom is **mostly empty space**.
**Some were deflected** through small angles: there is a **positive** charge concentrated in a small region that repels them.
**A very few bounced back** (deflected more than 90 degrees): the positive charge and most of the **mass** are concentrated in a **tiny nucleus**.
Plum pudding predicted that all alpha particles would pass through with only tiny deflections, so it was rejected.

callouts.p: In 4 and 6 mark questions, always pair each observation with what it shows about the atom.

core.p: Two numbers describe any nucleus. The **atomic number** identifies the element. The **mass number** tells you how many nucleons the nucleus contains.
bullets: **Atomic number (Z)**, also called **proton number**: the number of protons in the nucleus.
**Mass number (A)**, also called **nucleon number**: the total number of protons + neutrons.
**Number of neutrons = A - Z**.
In a neutral atom, **number of electrons = Z**.
All atoms of the same element have the **same atomic number**.

callouts.p: The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom.
The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom.

core.p: The **conventional representation** of a nucleus writes the element symbol with the **mass number at the top left** and the **atomic number at the bottom left**. In plain text this is written as, for example, 14 over 6 C, or as carbon-14 when only the mass number is needed.
bullets: Format: mass number A (top), atomic number Z (bottom), then symbol X.
Example: **carbon-14** has A = 14, Z = 6, so 6 protons and 14 - 6 = **8 neutrons**.
Example: **uranium-235** has A = 235, Z = 92, so 92 protons and **143 neutrons**.
The name form 'element-A' (e.g. uranium-238) gives the mass number only; you look up Z from the periodic table.
The bigger number is always the mass number.

callouts.p: Mass number is always the larger number (except hydrogen-1 where both are 1). If the top number is smaller you have them the wrong way round.

core.p: **Isotopes** are atoms of the **same element** (same number of protons) with **different numbers of neutrons**, so they have different mass numbers. They have the same chemical properties because they have the same number of electrons, but different nuclear properties such as mass and stability.
bullets: Same **atomic number**, different **mass number**.
Same number of **protons** and **electrons**; different number of **neutrons**.
Carbon-12, carbon-13 and carbon-14 are isotopes of carbon (all have 6 protons).
Hydrogen-1, hydrogen-2 (deuterium) and hydrogen-3 (tritium) are isotopes of hydrogen.
Some isotopes are **stable**; others are **unstable (radioactive)**, e.g. carbon-14 is radioactive but carbon-12 is stable.
Isotopes react chemically in the same way because chemistry depends on electrons.

callouts.p: Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.

core.p: Exam questions often give two or more nuclei in notation and ask whether they are isotopes, or ask for particle numbers. Compare the bottom numbers first.
bullets: **Same Z, different A**: isotopes of the same element.
**Different Z**: different elements, even if A is the same (e.g. carbon-14 and nitrogen-14).
Work out neutrons for each with **N = A - Z** to show the difference explicitly.
Isotopes differ in **nuclear mass** by the mass of the extra neutrons.

callouts.p: Carbon-14 (Z = 6) and nitrogen-14 (Z = 7) have the same mass number but are NOT isotopes; they are different elements.

core.p: Students often confuse ions and isotopes. Both are variations on an atom, but they change different particles.
bullets: **Isotope**: different number of **neutrons**; atom stays neutral; mass number changes.
**Ion**: different number of **electrons** from protons; has an overall **charge**; mass number unchanged.
Neither changes the number of protons, so both are still the **same element**.
Changing the number of protons makes a **different element** (this happens in some radioactive decays).

core.p: Most elements exist naturally as a **mixture of isotopes**. The relative atomic mass on the periodic table is a weighted average of the isotopes' masses, which is why many values are not whole numbers.
bullets: Chlorine is about 75% chlorine-35 and 25% chlorine-37, giving a relative atomic mass of about 35.5.
Isotopes of an element have **identical chemistry** so they cannot be separated by chemical reactions.
Unstable isotopes are called **radioisotopes** and emit nuclear radiation (covered in the next spec points).

core.p: This topic is high-scoring if you are precise with vocabulary and numbers.
bullets: Use **'protons and neutrons'** for the nucleus, not 'protons and electrons'.
Say the nucleus is **'small', 'dense' and 'positively charged'**.
Quote sizes with units: **1 x 10^-10 m** and **1 x 10^-15 m**.
Define isotopes using **both** 'same number of protons' and 'different number of neutrons'.
Show your working for neutrons: **N = A - Z**.

callouts.p: Many students lose a mark by only saying 'different number of neutrons'. Add 'same number of protons / same element'.

analogy.p: Picture an atom as a huge football stadium. The nucleus is a heavy marble on the centre spot, holding nearly all the mass, while the electrons are tiny midges flying around the outer stands. Everything else is empty space. Isotopes are like marbles made of the same number of red beads (protons) but different numbers of grey beads (neutrons): they belong to the same team (element) but weigh different amounts. Where it breaks down: electrons do not fly freely like midges but occupy fixed energy levels, and the nucleus is not a hard solid ball but a cluster of particles held by strong nuclear forces.

Thomson's model of the atom as a ball of positive charge with electrons embedded in it.

mistakes.w: The nucleus contains protons and electrons.
mistakes.r: The nucleus contains protons and neutrons; electrons are in shells around it.

mistakes.w: Isotopes have a different number of protons.
mistakes.r: Isotopes have the same number of protons and a different number of neutrons.

mistakes.w: Mass number is the number of neutrons.
mistakes.r: Mass number is the total number of protons plus neutrons.

mistakes.w: The nucleus is neutral.
mistakes.r: The nucleus is positively charged; the whole atom is neutral.

mistakes.w: The nucleus is about 10 times smaller than the atom.
mistakes.r: The nucleus radius (about 10^-15 m) is about 100 000 times smaller than the atom (about 10^-10 m).

mistakes.w: Most of the mass of an atom is in the electrons.
mistakes.r: Almost all of the mass is in the nucleus; electrons have very little mass.

mistakes.w: Carbon-14 and nitrogen-14 are isotopes because they have the same mass number.
mistakes.r: They have different atomic numbers, so they are different elements, not isotopes.

mistakes.w: Isotopes have different chemical properties.
mistakes.r: Isotopes have the same number of electrons so they have the same chemical properties.

exam.q: Name the two types of particle found in the nucleus.
model: Protons and neutrons.
exam.tip: Both needed for the mark.

exam.q: What is the relative charge of a neutron?
model: 0 (neutral).
exam.tip: Learn the full particle table.

exam.q: State the typical radius of an atom.
model: About 1 x 10^-10 m.
exam.tip: Include the unit and the negative power.

exam.q: Define the term isotopes.
model: Atoms of the same element / same number of protons.
With different numbers of neutrons.
exam.tip: Two parts, two marks.

exam.q: An atom of sodium is written with mass number 23 and atomic number 11. Calculate the number of protons, neutrons and electrons.
model: Protons = 11 and electrons = 11.
Neutrons = 23 - 11 = 12.
exam.tip: Show N = A - Z.

exam.q: Explain why an atom has no overall charge.
model: It has equal numbers of protons and electrons.
The positive and negative charges are equal and opposite, so they cancel.
exam.tip: Mention equal numbers and equal size of charge.

exam.q: Describe the structure of an atom, including the relative sizes of the atom and nucleus and where the mass is.
model: A small positively charged nucleus at the centre containing protons and neutrons.
Negatively charged electrons around the nucleus in energy levels / shells.
Nucleus radius about 10^-15 m, atom radius about 10^-10 m (nucleus about 100 000 times smaller).
Almost all the mass is in the nucleus.
exam.tip: Hit structure, charge, size and mass for four marks.

exam.q: Uranium-235 and uranium-238 are isotopes of uranium (atomic number 92). Compare their nuclei.
model: Both have 92 protons.
Uranium-235 has 143 neutrons.
Uranium-238 has 146 neutrons.
So uranium-238 has 3 more neutrons / a greater nuclear mass; same chemical properties.
exam.tip: Calculate neutrons for both and state the difference.

exam.q: Explain how the results of the alpha scattering experiment led to the nuclear model of the atom replacing the plum pudding model.
model: Alpha particles (positive) were fired at thin gold foil.
Most passed straight through, so the atom is mostly empty space.
Some were deflected, so there is a concentrated region of positive charge that repels them.
A few bounced back, so most of the mass and charge is concentrated in a very small nucleus.
The plum pudding model predicted only tiny deflections with spread-out positive charge, so it could not explain the results.
So the nuclear model (small dense positive nucleus with electrons around it) replaced it.
exam.tip: Pair each observation with its conclusion and finish with why the old model was rejected.

worked.q: Chlorine has two isotopes, chlorine-35 and chlorine-37. The atomic number of chlorine is 17. Find the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in a neutral atom of each.
steps: Both isotopes are chlorine, so Z = 17: 17 protons.
Neutral atom: electrons = protons = 17.
Chlorine-35: neutrons = A - Z = 35 - 17 = 18.
Chlorine-37: neutrons = 37 - 17 = 20.
worked.ans: Chlorine-35: 17 p, 18 n, 17 e. Chlorine-37: 17 p, 20 n, 17 e.

worked.q: The radius of a gold atom is about 1.4 x 10^-10 m and the radius of its nucleus is about 7 x 10^-15 m. How many times bigger is the atom than the nucleus?
steps: Ratio = atom radius / nucleus radius.
worked.ans: The atom is about 20 000 times larger in radius than the nucleus.

worked.q: Four nuclei are given as (A, Z): P (14, 6), Q (14, 7), R (12, 6), S (16, 8). Which two are isotopes of the same element?
steps: Isotopes must have the same atomic number Z.
P has Z = 6 and R has Z = 6; Q has Z = 7; S has Z = 8.
P and R have the same Z but different A (14 and 12).
P and Q share A = 14 but different Z, so they are different elements.
worked.ans: P and R are isotopes (both carbon: carbon-14 and carbon-12).

phy_ocra.14.1.summary: Some nuclei are **unstable** and become more stable by emitting nuclear radiation: **alpha particles**, **beta particles**, **gamma rays** or **neutrons**. Each emission changes the nucleus in a predictable way: alpha lowers the mass number by 4 and the atomic number by 2, beta keeps the mass number and raises the atomic number by 1, gamma changes neither, and neutron emission lowers the mass number by 1. In a **balanced nuclear equation** the mass numbers and the atomic numbers on each side must add up to the same totals, which lets you work out unknown nuclei.

core.p: Some isotopes have nuclei that are **unstable** because they have too many neutrons, too many protons, or are simply too big. These nuclei **decay** randomly by emitting radiation from the nucleus to become more stable. This process is called **radioactive decay**, and the material is **radioactive**.
bullets: Radiation comes from the **nucleus**, not from the electrons.
Decay is **random**: you cannot predict when a particular nucleus will decay.
The original nucleus is called the **parent**; the nucleus left behind is the **daughter**.
After alpha or beta decay the daughter is a **different element** because the number of protons changes.
The four emissions OCR requires: **alpha, beta, gamma and neutron**.

callouts.p: The random process in which an unstable nucleus emits radiation (alpha, beta, gamma or neutrons) to become more stable.

core.p: Learn this table thoroughly: it is the core of almost every question on this point.
bullets: Alpha and beta are **particles**; gamma is **electromagnetic radiation**; a neutron is a neutral **particle**.
Only alpha and beta change the **element** (they change Z).
Gamma changes only the **energy** of the nucleus.
Neutron emission makes a **different isotope** of the same element.

callouts.p: Alpha: mass and charge both change. Beta: only charge changes. Gamma: neither changes. Neutron: only mass changes.

core.p: An **alpha particle** is a **helium nucleus**: 2 protons and 2 neutrons bound together. When a nucleus emits one, it loses 4 nucleons and 2 protons, so its **mass number falls by 4** and its **atomic number falls by 2**. The daughter is an element two places earlier in the periodic table.
bullets: Alpha particle: mass number **4**, atomic number **2**, charge **+2**.
Usually emitted by **large, heavy nuclei** such as uranium, radium, polonium and americium.
Example: uranium-238 (Z = 92) decays to thorium-234 (Z = 90) by alpha emission.
Check: top 238 = 234 + 4; bottom 92 = 90 + 2.

callouts.p: A particle made of two protons and two neutrons (a helium nucleus) emitted from an unstable nucleus.

core.p: In **beta decay** a **neutron in the nucleus changes into a proton and an electron**. The proton stays in the nucleus and the electron is emitted at high speed as a **beta particle**. The total number of nucleons stays the same, but there is one more proton.
bullets: Beta particle: a **fast-moving electron** from the nucleus; mass number **0**, charge **-1**.
Neutron -> proton + electron.
**Mass number unchanged**; **atomic number increases by 1**.
The daughter is the element one place **later** in the periodic table.
Usually emitted by nuclei with **too many neutrons**.
Example: carbon-14 (Z = 6) -> nitrogen-14 (Z = 7) + beta: 14/6 C -> 14/7 N + 0/-1 e.

callouts.p: A beta particle is created in the nucleus when a neutron changes; it is not one of the atom's shell electrons.
A high-speed electron emitted from the nucleus when a neutron changes into a proton.

core.p: **Gamma rays** are **high-frequency electromagnetic waves** emitted when a nucleus loses excess **energy**. Often after an alpha or beta decay the daughter nucleus is left in an **excited state** with extra energy, and it releases this as a gamma ray.
bullets: Gamma has **no mass and no charge**: written 0/0 gamma.
**Mass number and atomic number do not change**, so the element stays the same.
Only the **energy** of the nucleus decreases.
Gamma emission usually **accompanies** alpha or beta decay.
Example: cobalt-60 emits gamma rays (along with beta) and is used in radiotherapy and sterilising equipment.

callouts.t: Gamma changes nothing in the equation
callouts.p: Adding a gamma ray to a nuclear equation does not change either total, because it has A = 0 and Z = 0.

fig.cap: Gamma emission. An excited nucleus loses energy by emitting a gamma ray (an electromagnetic wave). Mass number and atomic number stay the same.

core.p: Some very neutron-rich nuclei become more stable by emitting a **single neutron**. Since a neutron has a mass number of 1 and no charge, the **mass number falls by 1** and the **atomic number stays the same**, so the daughter is a **different isotope of the same element**.
bullets: Neutron symbol: **1/0 n** (A = 1, Z = 0).
**A decreases by 1**, **Z unchanged**.
Same element, lighter isotope.
Example: helium-5 -> helium-4 + neutron: 5/2 He -> 4/2 He + 1/0 n.
Free neutrons are also released in **nuclear fission**; neutron radiation can make other materials radioactive.

callouts.p: If Z does not change, the symbol does not change; only the mass number goes down by 1.

core.p: Each particle and nucleus in a decay equation is written with its **mass number (A) on top** and **atomic number (Z) underneath**. In these notes they are written in plain text as A/Z followed by the symbol, for example 4/2 He.
bullets: Alpha: **4/2 He** (or 4/2 alpha).
Beta: **0/-1 e** (or 0/-1 beta). The -1 is its charge acting as an atomic number.
Gamma: **0/0 gamma**.
Neutron: **1/0 n**.
Proton (sometimes needed): **1/1 p**.

callouts.p: The atomic number of a beta particle is -1, not 1 and not 0. This is what makes Z go up by 1 in the daughter.

core.p: In every nuclear equation **two totals are conserved**: the **sum of mass numbers** and the **sum of atomic numbers** must be the same on both sides. This lets you find any one unknown number or symbol.
bullets: Rule 1: total of **top numbers (A)** on the left = total on the right.
Rule 2: total of **bottom numbers (Z)** on the left = total on the right.
Find the missing Z first, then use the **periodic table** to name the element from Z.
Mass number is conserved because nucleons are not created or destroyed (in beta a neutron just becomes a proton).
Charge is conserved: in beta decay, the new +1 proton and the -1 electron cancel to give zero net change.

callouts.p: Mass number and atomic number (charge) are both conserved in nuclear equations.
The element symbol is fixed by Z, not A. If Z changes, the symbol must change.

core.p: Practise these patterns so you can recognise each type of decay from its equation.
bullets: Alpha: 226/88 Ra -> 222/86 Rn + 4/2 He (radium to radon).
Alpha: 241/95 Am -> 237/93 Np + 4/2 He (americium in smoke detectors).
Beta: 90/38 Sr -> 90/39 Y + 0/-1 e (strontium to yttrium).
Beta: 131/53 I -> 131/54 Xe + 0/-1 e (iodine-131 used in medicine).
Gamma: an excited nucleus emits 0/0 gamma with no change in A or Z.
Neutron: 5/2 He -> 4/2 He + 1/0 n.

core.h: Identifying the decay from the change
core.p: Questions may give the parent and daughter and ask which radiation was emitted. Work out the changes in A and Z.
bullets: A down 4, Z down 2: **alpha**.
A same, Z up 1: **beta**.
A same, Z same, energy lost: **gamma**.
A down 1, Z same: **neutron**.
Multi-step chains: add up the effects, e.g. one alpha then two beta decays gives A down 4 and Z back to the original value (a new isotope of the original element).

core.p: Nuclei decay towards a more stable balance of protons and neutrons. Understanding why helps you predict the type of decay.
bullets: **Too heavy** (very large nuclei): alpha decay removes 4 nucleons in one go.
**Too many neutrons**: beta decay turns a neutron into a proton, improving the balance.
**Very neutron-rich**: a neutron may be emitted directly.
**Too much energy** after a decay: gamma emission carries the excess energy away.
Each process **releases energy**, carried as kinetic energy of the particle or as the gamma ray.

core.p: Balanced-equation questions are usually quick marks if you set them out clearly.
bullets: Write the full equation with **both numbers** on every symbol.
Show your two balancing sums (top and bottom) as working.
State the effect on the nucleus in words: e.g. **'mass number decreases by 4 and atomic number decreases by 2'**.
For beta, say **'a neutron changes into a proton and an electron; the electron is emitted'**.
Remember gamma is **electromagnetic radiation**, not a particle.

callouts.p: Add up the tops and bottoms on each side. If they do not match, your equation is wrong.

analogy.t: The nucleus as a crowded lifeboat
analogy.p: Think of an unstable nucleus as an overloaded lifeboat trying to become stable. Alpha decay is throwing a tied-together group of four people (two crew in red, two passengers in grey) overboard: the boat gets lighter by 4 and loses 2 crew. Beta decay is one passenger putting on a crew uniform and throwing their old coat overboard: the head count stays the same but there is one more crew member. Gamma emission is the boat shaking off nervous energy by letting out a shout: nobody leaves. Neutron emission is one passenger jumping off alone: lighter by one, same crew. Where it breaks down: in a real nucleus nobody chooses to leave, decay is completely random, and the 'coat' in beta decay is a brand new electron created in the change, not something the neutron was carrying.

terms.d: A nucleus that can decay by emitting radiation to become more stable.
The random emission of radiation from an unstable nucleus.
The original nucleus before it decays.
The nucleus left after a decay.
Two protons and two neutrons (a helium nucleus), symbol 4/2 He, charge +2.
A fast-moving electron emitted from the nucleus when a neutron changes into a proton, symbol 0/-1 e.
High-frequency electromagnetic radiation emitted from a nucleus losing energy; no mass or charge.
Decay in which a nucleus ejects a neutron, lowering the mass number by 1.
Number of protons plus neutrons in a nucleus.
Number of protons in a nucleus; fixes the element.
An equation in which the total mass numbers and total atomic numbers are equal on both sides.
A nucleus with excess energy that it can release as a gamma ray.
Alpha, beta, gamma or neutron radiation emitted from unstable nuclei.
Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons.

mistakes.w: In alpha decay the atomic number decreases by 4.
mistakes.r: The mass number decreases by 4 and the atomic number decreases by 2.

mistakes.w: In beta decay the mass number decreases by 1.
mistakes.r: The mass number is unchanged and the atomic number increases by 1.

mistakes.w: A beta particle is an electron from the outer shell.
mistakes.r: A beta particle is an electron created in the nucleus when a neutron changes into a proton.

mistakes.w: Gamma emission changes the element.
mistakes.r: Gamma has no mass or charge, so A and Z are unchanged; it only removes energy.

mistakes.w: Writing the beta particle as 0/1 e or 0/0 e.
mistakes.r: Beta particle is written 0/-1 e.

mistakes.w: Keeping the same element symbol after alpha or beta decay.
mistakes.r: Z changes, so the daughter is a different element with a new symbol.

mistakes.w: Neutron emission changes the atomic number.
mistakes.r: A neutron has Z = 0, so the atomic number is unchanged and only A decreases by 1.

mistakes.w: Not balancing the bottom numbers of the equation.
mistakes.r: Both the mass numbers and the atomic numbers must balance on each side.

exam.q: What is an alpha particle made of?
model: Two protons and two neutrons (a helium nucleus).
exam.tip: Helium nucleus alone is accepted; helium atom is not.

exam.q: State what happens in the nucleus during beta decay.
model: A neutron changes into a proton and an electron.
The electron is emitted (as the beta particle).
exam.tip: Name both new particles.

exam.q: What happens to the mass number and atomic number of a nucleus that emits a gamma ray?
model: Both stay the same / no change.
exam.tip: Gamma only removes energy.

exam.q: Write the symbol for a beta particle showing its mass number and atomic number.
model: 0/-1 e (mass number 0, atomic number -1).
exam.tip: The bottom number is -1.

exam.q: Polonium-210 (Z = 84) decays by alpha emission to lead (Pb). Write the balanced equation.
model: Correct numbers for Pb: A = 206, Z = 82.

exam.q: Complete the equation: 14/6 C -> ?/? N + 0/-1 e.
model: Mass number of N = 14.
Atomic number of N = 7.
exam.tip: Bottom: 6 = Z + (-1), so Z = 7.

exam.q: A nucleus emits a neutron. Describe the effect on its mass number, atomic number and the element.
model: Mass number decreases by 1; atomic number unchanged.
So it is the same element (a different isotope).
exam.tip: Link unchanged Z to same element.

exam.q: Compare the changes to a nucleus caused by alpha, beta and gamma emission.
model: Alpha: mass number decreases by 4.
Alpha: atomic number decreases by 2 (charge and mass both change).
Beta: mass number unchanged, atomic number increases by 1 (only charge changes).
Gamma: no change to mass number or atomic number; nucleus loses energy.
exam.tip: Use a sentence or row per radiation.

exam.q: Uranium-238 (Z = 92) decays by alpha emission, and the daughter then decays by beta emission. Find the mass number and atomic number of the final nucleus.
model: After alpha: A = 238 - 4 = 234.
After alpha: Z = 92 - 2 = 90 (thorium).
After beta: A stays 234.
After beta: Z = 90 + 1 = 91 (protactinium).
exam.tip: Track A and Z separately step by step.

exam.q: Explain how alpha, beta, gamma and neutron emissions change the mass and charge of a nucleus, and how balanced nuclear equations show this. Use examples.
model: Alpha particle is 2 protons + 2 neutrons; nucleus loses mass (A down 4) and charge (Z down 2), e.g. U-238 to Th-234.
Beta: a neutron turns into a proton and an electron which is emitted; Z up 1, A unchanged, e.g. C-14 to N-14.
Gamma: electromagnetic radiation, no mass or charge; A and Z unchanged, only energy lost.
Neutron emission: A down 1, Z unchanged, same element (new isotope).
In balanced equations the total mass numbers are equal on both sides.
And the total atomic numbers are equal on both sides; the element is identified from Z.
exam.tip: Give each emission with its effect and one example, then explain the two conservation rules.

worked.q: Radium-226 (Z = 88) decays by alpha emission. Find the mass number and atomic number of the daughter and identify it (Z = 86 is radon).
steps: Write the equation: 226/88 Ra -> A/Z X + 4/2 He.
Top numbers: 226 = A + 4, so A = 222.
Bottom numbers: 88 = Z + 2, so Z = 86.
Z = 86 is radon, Rn.
worked.ans: 226/88 Ra -> 222/86 Rn + 4/2 He; the daughter is radon-222.

worked.q: Iodine-131 (Z = 53) decays by beta emission. Find the daughter nucleus (Z = 54 is xenon).
steps: Write the equation: 131/53 I -> A/Z X + 0/-1 e.
Bottom: 53 = Z + (-1), so Z = 54.
Z = 54 is xenon.
worked.ans: 131/53 I -> 131/54 Xe + 0/-1 e; the daughter is xenon-131.

worked.q: A nucleus X changes into 234/91 Pa by emitting one beta particle. What was X? (Z = 90 is thorium.)
steps: Equation: A/Z X -> 234/91 Pa + 0/-1 e.
Z = 90 is thorium.

phy_ocra.14.2.summary: Electrons in an atom can only exist at certain **fixed energy levels** (shells) at set distances from the nucleus. When an atom **absorbs electromagnetic radiation** an electron can jump to a higher level (**excitation**) or leave the atom completely (**ionisation**, forming a positive ion). When an excited electron falls back to a lower level the atom **emits electromagnetic radiation** whose energy and frequency exactly match the gap between the levels, which is why each element has its own unique line spectrum.

core.h: Electrons sit in fixed energy levels
core.p: In the nuclear model of the atom, the tiny positive nucleus is surrounded by negatively charged electrons. These electrons cannot have just any energy: they occupy **discrete energy levels** (also called shells or orbits) at **fixed distances from the nucleus**. An electron further from the nucleus has **more energy** than one closer in.
bullets: Energy levels are **fixed (quantised)**: an electron is either in one level or another, never in between.
The level closest to the nucleus is the **lowest energy level** (ground state).
Levels further out have **higher energy**; the gaps between levels get smaller further from the nucleus.
The arrangement of levels is **different for every element**, because each element has a different number of protons and electrons.
Electrons are held in the atom by the **electrostatic attraction** to the positive nucleus; moving outwards means doing work against this attraction, so energy must be supplied.

callouts.p: A fixed amount of energy an electron in an atom can have, corresponding to a particular distance (shell) from the nucleus.
An electron must gain energy to move to a level further from the nucleus and must lose energy to move closer.

core.p: Atoms can **absorb electromagnetic (EM) radiation**, such as visible light or ultraviolet. The energy carried by the radiation is transferred to an electron. If the energy absorbed is exactly right, the electron moves up to a higher energy level further from the nucleus.
bullets: Absorbing EM radiation **increases the energy** of an electron.
The electron moves to a **higher energy level, further from the nucleus**.
Only radiation with energy that **exactly matches the gap** between two levels can cause a jump between those levels.
Higher-frequency radiation carries **more energy**, so it can cause bigger jumps (for example ultraviolet compared with infrared).
Electrons can also gain energy by **heating** or by **collisions** with other particles (e.g. in a discharge tube), but the spec focuses on EM radiation.

callouts.p: Write 'the electron absorbs electromagnetic radiation and moves to a higher energy level further from the nucleus' for full marks.

core.p: When an electron absorbs energy and moves to a higher energy level but **stays in the atom**, the atom is said to be **excited**. This state is unstable, so the electron will soon fall back down again.
bullets: Excitation = electron moves **up** one or more levels and **remains in the atom**.
The atom is still **neutral**: no electrons have been lost.
An excited atom is **unstable**; the electron usually returns to a lower level very quickly.
The amount of energy needed equals the **difference in energy** between the two levels.

callouts.p: When an electron absorbs energy and moves to a higher energy level, further from the nucleus, without leaving the atom.

core.p: If an outer electron absorbs **enough energy**, it does not just move up a level: it **leaves the atom completely**. The atom has then lost a negative charge and becomes a **positive ion**. This is ionisation.
bullets: Ionisation = an atom **loses (or gains) an electron**, so it becomes **charged** (an ion).
When an electron is removed, the atom has **more protons than electrons**, so it becomes a **positive ion**.
Outer electrons are easiest to remove because they are **furthest from the nucleus** and least strongly attracted.
Ionisation needs **more energy** than any excitation from the same starting level.
**Ionising radiation** (alpha, beta, gamma, X-rays, high-energy UV) is radiation with enough energy to knock electrons out of atoms.

callouts.p: When an atom loses (or gains) one or more electrons, becoming a charged ion. Losing an outer electron leaves a positive ion.
Losing an electron makes the atom POSITIVE, not negative. Electrons are negative, so taking one away leaves more positive charge.

core.p: Both processes start with an electron absorbing energy. The difference is whether the electron stays in the atom or escapes.
bullets: Small energy absorbed that matches a gap: **excitation**.
Large energy absorbed, enough to escape: **ionisation**.
Excitation leaves a **neutral atom**; ionisation leaves a **positive ion** and a free electron.

core.p: An excited electron does not stay up for long. When it **falls back to a lower energy level** (closer to the nucleus) it **loses energy**, and that energy is carried away from the atom as **electromagnetic radiation**.
bullets: Electron moves **down** a level = atom **emits** EM radiation.
The energy emitted **equals the energy difference** between the two levels.
A **large drop** emits high-energy, **high-frequency** radiation (e.g. ultraviolet or blue/violet light).
A **small drop** emits lower-energy, **lower-frequency** radiation (e.g. red light or infrared).
An electron may fall back in **one big jump or several smaller jumps**, so several different frequencies can be emitted from the same excitation.

Changes in energy levels of electrons can produce radiation across a **wide range of frequencies**, from infrared through visible to ultraviolet; inner-electron transitions in heavy atoms can produce X-rays.

callouts.p: Electron falls to a lower energy level, closer to the nucleus, and the atom emits electromagnetic radiation.

core.h: Energy, frequency and the size of the jump
core.p: The energy carried by EM radiation is linked to its **frequency**: higher frequency means more energy. Because energy levels are fixed, the energy lost in a particular drop is always the same, so the frequency (and colour) of the radiation emitted is always the same for that drop.
bullets: Bigger energy gap between levels means **higher frequency** and **shorter wavelength** radiation.
Smaller energy gap means **lower frequency** and **longer wavelength**.
In the visible region, frequency is seen as **colour**: violet is highest frequency, red is lowest.
All EM radiation travels at the **same speed in a vacuum** (3 x 10^8 m/s), so higher frequency always means shorter wavelength (wave speed = frequency x wavelength).

core.h: Why each element has a unique line spectrum
core.p: Because each element has its **own set of energy levels**, the gaps between them are unique. When the excited atoms of an element emit light, only **specific frequencies** appear. Passed through a prism or diffraction grating, this light shows as a set of **bright coloured lines** on a dark background: an **emission line spectrum**.
bullets: Each line corresponds to **one particular electron drop** between two levels.
The pattern of lines acts like a **fingerprint** for the element.
If white light passes through a cool gas, the gas **absorbs** the same specific frequencies, giving **dark lines** on a continuous spectrum (absorption spectrum).
The dark absorption lines are in **exactly the same positions** as the bright emission lines for that element, because the same energy gaps are involved.
Astronomers use line spectra to identify the **elements present in stars**; this is how helium was first discovered in the Sun.

callouts.p: Absorption and emission lines of an element sit at identical frequencies because both are caused by electrons moving between the same pair of fixed energy levels.

core.p: The spec links electron energy levels to **ionising radiation** from the nucleus. Alpha, beta and gamma radiation carry enough energy to **ionise** atoms they pass through by knocking electrons out. Gamma rays are themselves EM radiation, but they come from changes **in the nucleus**, not from electron energy levels.
bullets: **Ionising radiation** = radiation with enough energy to remove electrons from atoms.
Alpha particles are the **most strongly ionising**; gamma rays are the **least ionising** of the three.
Ionisation of atoms in living cells can **damage DNA**, which is why ionising radiation is hazardous.
Visible light and infrared are **not ionising**: their energy is too small to remove an electron.
High-frequency **ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays** are ionising EM radiation.

callouts.p: Light, UV and X-rays can come from electron level changes; gamma rays come from the nucleus after radioactive decay. Do not say gamma rays are caused by electrons moving between levels.

core.h: Linking to the development of the atomic model
core.p: **Niels Bohr** proposed that electrons orbit the nucleus at **specific distances** (fixed energy levels). His model was accepted because it explained why atoms emit and absorb only specific frequencies of light, matching the observed line spectra.
bullets: Bohr's theoretical calculations **agreed with experimental observations** of hydrogen's spectrum.
This is an example of how **new evidence** leads scientists to change a model.
The energy level model builds on Rutherford's nuclear model (tiny positive nucleus, electrons outside).

core.h: Using energy level diagrams in the exam
core.p: Questions often show a set of horizontal lines (energy levels) and arrows. You must decide what each arrow represents and compare energies or frequencies.
bullets: Arrow **upwards** = absorption of energy (excitation).
Arrow **downwards** = emission of EM radiation.
Arrow from a level to the top (off the diagram) = **ionisation**.
**Longer arrow** = more energy = higher frequency = shorter wavelength.
Count possible drops: an electron in level 3 could drop 3 to 2, 2 to 1, or 3 to 1, giving **three different lines**.

callouts.p: When asked which transition emits the highest frequency, pick the longest downward arrow and say why: it has the largest energy change.

analogy.p: Think of the electron as a person standing on a ladder whose rungs are the energy levels. To climb you must be given exactly enough energy to reach a rung; you cannot stand between rungs (excitation). Given a huge boost, you leap off the top of the ladder and leave entirely (ionisation). Stepping down a rung releases energy as a flash of light, and a bigger step down gives a more energetic, higher-frequency flash (emission). Where it breaks down: real ladder rungs are evenly spaced, but energy levels get closer together further from the nucleus, and electrons do not physically climb through the space between levels; they simply change from one level to another.

terms.d: A fixed energy an electron in an atom can have, linked to a particular distance from the nucleus.
Another name for an energy level in which electrons are found around the nucleus.
The lowest energy arrangement of electrons in an atom.
An electron absorbing energy and moving to a higher energy level while staying in the atom.
An atom in which one or more electrons are in a higher energy level than normal; it is unstable.
An atom losing or gaining electrons so that it becomes a charged ion.
An atom that has lost one or more electrons, so it has more protons than electrons.
Energy from electromagnetic radiation being taken in by an electron, raising it to a higher level.
Release of electromagnetic radiation when an electron falls to a lower energy level.
Transverse waves that transfer energy, travel at 3 x 10^8 m/s in a vacuum and include radio waves to gamma rays.
The number of waves passing a point each second, measured in hertz (Hz); higher frequency EM radiation carries more energy.
A pattern of specific frequencies (lines) emitted or absorbed by an element, unique to that element.
A continuous spectrum crossed by dark lines where an element has absorbed specific frequencies.
Radiation with enough energy to remove electrons from atoms, such as alpha, beta, gamma, X-rays and high-energy UV.
Atomic model in which electrons orbit the nucleus at fixed distances corresponding to fixed energy levels.

mistakes.w: When an atom loses an electron it becomes a negative ion.
mistakes.r: Losing a negative electron leaves more protons than electrons, so it becomes a positive ion.

mistakes.w: Electrons emit radiation when they move to a higher energy level.
mistakes.r: Electrons absorb radiation to move up; they emit radiation when they fall to a lower level.

mistakes.w: Excitation means the electron leaves the atom.
mistakes.r: Excitation: electron moves to a higher level but stays in the atom. Leaving the atom is ionisation.

mistakes.w: Electrons further from the nucleus have less energy.
mistakes.r: Electrons further from the nucleus are in higher energy levels and have more energy.

mistakes.w: Any amount of light energy can make an electron move up.
mistakes.r: Only energy exactly equal to the gap between levels causes a jump (or enough to ionise).

mistakes.w: A small energy drop gives high frequency light.
mistakes.r: A larger energy drop gives higher frequency radiation; a small drop gives low frequency.

mistakes.w: Gamma rays are produced when electrons change energy levels.
mistakes.r: Gamma rays are emitted from unstable nuclei; electron transitions give light, UV and X-rays.

mistakes.w: All elements give the same spectrum lines.
mistakes.r: Each element has unique energy levels so its spectral lines are at unique frequencies.

exam.q: State what happens to an electron when an atom absorbs electromagnetic radiation.
model: The electron gains energy
and moves to a higher energy level / further from the nucleus
exam.tip: Always link energy gain with the direction of movement.

exam.q: State what is meant by ionisation.
model: An atom loses (or gains) an electron so it becomes charged / an ion
exam.tip: Mention charge or ion explicitly.

exam.q: An atom loses an outer electron. What is the charge on the particle formed?
model: Positive (+1)
exam.tip: Electron removed means positive.

exam.q: Describe how an atom emits electromagnetic radiation.
model: An electron falls/moves from a higher energy level to a lower energy level (closer to nucleus)
Energy is released as electromagnetic radiation
exam.tip: Use 'lower energy level', not just 'moves down'.

exam.q: Explain the difference between excitation and ionisation.
model: Excitation: electron moves to a higher energy level but stays in the atom
Ionisation: electron gains enough energy to leave the atom, forming an ion
exam.tip: Make a clear comparison of whether the electron stays.

exam.q: An electron falls from level 3 to level 1 and another falls from level 3 to level 2. Explain which emits radiation of higher frequency.
model: Level 3 to level 1
because it has the larger energy change / larger gap
exam.tip: Link bigger energy drop to higher frequency.

exam.q: An electron is in energy level 3 of an atom. How many different frequencies of radiation could be emitted as it returns to level 1?
model: Three (3 to 2, 2 to 1, 3 to 1)
exam.tip: List the possible drops to check.

exam.q: Explain why the light emitted by heated sodium contains only certain frequencies.
model: Electrons can only occupy fixed/discrete energy levels
Electrons are excited to higher levels then fall back
Each fall releases energy equal to the difference between two levels
Only certain energy differences exist, so only certain frequencies are emitted
exam.tip: Fixed levels gives fixed energy gaps gives fixed frequencies: build the chain.

exam.q: Explain why ultraviolet radiation can ionise atoms but infrared radiation cannot.
model: Ultraviolet has a higher frequency so carries more energy
Enough energy to remove an electron from the atom; infrared does not have enough
exam.tip: Frequency links to energy; energy links to ionisation.

exam.q: Describe and explain how electrons in atoms absorb and emit electromagnetic radiation, and how this can be used to identify elements in a star.
model: Electrons occupy fixed energy levels at set distances from the nucleus
Absorbing EM radiation of the right energy moves an electron to a higher level (excitation)
If enough energy is absorbed the electron leaves the atom (ionisation, positive ion)
Electron falling to a lower level emits EM radiation with energy equal to the gap
Each element has unique energy levels so emits/absorbs unique frequencies (line spectrum)
Dark absorption lines in starlight are matched to known element spectra to identify the elements
exam.tip: Level 3 answers cover absorption, emission AND the application with linked reasoning.

worked.q: An atom has four energy levels. An electron is excited to level 4. Work out how many different spectral lines could be produced as it returns to level 1, and identify which gives the highest and lowest frequency.
steps: List all possible downward transitions: 4-3, 4-2, 4-1, 3-2, 3-1, 2-1.
That gives 6 different transitions, so up to 6 lines.
Highest frequency: largest energy gap, which is 4 to 1.
Lowest frequency: smallest gap; levels get closer together further out, so 4 to 3.
worked.ans: 6 possible lines; 4 to 1 gives highest frequency, 4 to 3 gives lowest frequency.

worked.q: Model answer: Explain why a helium atom can absorb some frequencies of light but not others.
steps: Electrons in helium can only be in fixed energy levels.
To move up, an electron must absorb exactly the energy of the gap between two levels.
Energy of EM radiation depends on its frequency.
So only frequencies whose energy matches a gap are absorbed; others pass straight through.
worked.ans: Only light with energy exactly equal to an energy level gap is absorbed, so only certain frequencies are absorbed.

worked.q: Applied example: Explain what happens to a neutral atom hit by a beta particle that removes an outer electron.
steps: The beta particle transfers energy to an outer electron.
The electron gains enough energy to escape the attraction of the nucleus.
The atom now has one more proton than electrons.
So it becomes a positive ion: this is ionisation.
worked.ans: The atom is ionised, becoming a positive ion with a charge of +1, and a free electron is released.

phy_ocra.14.3.summary: Radioactive decay is **random**: you cannot predict when any single unstable nucleus will decay, but with huge numbers of nuclei the overall pattern is very predictable. The **half-life** of an isotope is the time taken for the number of unstable nuclei (or the activity) of a sample to **halve**. Using half-life you can predict how activity or count rate falls over time, read half-lives from decay graphs, and (Higher tier) calculate the net decline as a ratio after a number of half-lives.

core.p: An unstable nucleus becomes more stable by emitting radiation. This process is **random**: it is impossible to predict **which** nucleus will decay next or **when** a particular nucleus will decay. Each nucleus has the same fixed chance of decaying in a given time.
bullets: Decay is **spontaneous**: it is not triggered by anything outside the nucleus.
It is **not affected** by temperature, pressure or chemical bonding.
Each nucleus of a given isotope has the **same probability** of decaying per second.
Because samples contain **billions of nuclei**, the random behaviour averages out and the overall rate of decay is predictable.
Evidence for randomness: count rates from a source **fluctuate** around an average from one reading to the next.

callouts.p: It is not possible to predict which nucleus will decay or when a particular nucleus will decay; only the probability of decay can be known.
Do not say nuclei decay one after another in order, or that the oldest nuclei decay first. Every undecayed nucleus has the same chance.

core.p: The **activity** of a source is the number of nuclei that decay per second. It is measured in **becquerels (Bq)**, where 1 Bq = 1 decay per second. In practice we measure **count rate** with a Geiger-Muller tube and counter.
bullets: Activity is **proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei**: more unstable nuclei means more decays per second.
As nuclei decay, there are fewer left, so the **activity falls** over time.
**Count rate** is the number of decays detected per second (or per minute) by a detector.
Count rate is **lower than activity** because some radiation travels away from the detector or is absorbed.
Always **subtract background radiation** from measured count rates before working out half-life.

callouts.p: The rate at which a source of unstable nuclei decays, measured in becquerels (Bq).
The number of decays recorded each second (or minute) by a detector such as a Geiger-Muller tube.

core.p: The **half-life** is a property of each isotope. It tells you how quickly the sample decays. It can be defined in two equivalent ways, and both are rewarded in mark schemes.
bullets: Definition 1: the time taken for the **number of unstable (undecayed) nuclei** in a sample to **halve**.
Definition 2: the time taken for the **count rate (or activity)** of a sample to fall to **half its initial value**.
Half-life is **constant** for a given isotope: it takes the same time to go from 800 to 400 as from 400 to 200.
Half-lives range from fractions of a second to **billions of years**.
Half-life **does not depend on the amount** of the sample.

callouts.p: The time taken for half the unstable nuclei in a sample to decay, or the time taken for the count rate (activity) to halve.
Half-life is not half the time for the whole sample to decay. A sample never completely decays in a simple number of half-lives.

core.h: Why the decay curve has its shape
core.p: Because each nucleus has a fixed chance of decaying, the **number that decay** per second is proportional to the **number left**. At first there are many nuclei, so many decay and the graph falls steeply. Later there are few left, so fewer decay and the graph levels off. This gives an **exponential decay curve**.
bullets: The curve **never reaches zero** in theory; it gets closer and closer.
Every half-life, the value **halves**: 100%, 50%, 25%, 12.5%, 6.25%...
The **gradient** (rate of decay) is steepest at the start and decreases over time.
The same shape applies to number of nuclei, activity and count rate (corrected for background).

core.p: This is one of the most common exam skills. You read off the time it takes for the value on the y-axis to halve.
bullets: Step 1: read the **starting value** on the y-axis (e.g. 800 counts/min).
Step 2: **halve it** (400) and draw a horizontal line across to the curve.
Step 3: draw a vertical line down to the time axis and **read the time**.
Step 4: check by repeating from 400 to 200: the time taken should be the **same**.
You can start from **any point**, not just time zero, e.g. from 600 to 300.
For accuracy, take **several half-life readings** and find a mean.

core.h: Calculating with whole numbers of half-lives
core.p: If you know the half-life, you can work out how much remains after a given time by **halving repeatedly**. First work out **how many half-lives** have passed: number of half-lives = time elapsed / half-life.
bullets: After 1 half-life: **1/2** remains.
After 2 half-lives: **1/4** remains.
After 3 half-lives: **1/8** remains.
After n half-lives: **(1/2)^n** remains.
Amount remaining = initial amount x (1/2)^n.
To find half-life from data: count how many halvings occurred, then half-life = total time / number of halvings.

callouts.p: Read the question carefully: 'how much has decayed' is 1 minus the fraction remaining.

core.h: Net decline as a ratio (Higher tier)
core.p: Higher tier students must be able to calculate the **net decline**, expressed as a **ratio**, in a radioactive emission after a given (whole) number of half-lives. The ratio compares the final activity (or number of nuclei) with the initial value.
bullets: After n half-lives, ratio of final to initial = **1 : 2^n**.
After 3 half-lives, activity has fallen to 1/8, so the ratio final : initial = **1 : 8**.
Net decline = initial minus final; as a ratio of initial, **net decline = 1 - (1/2)^n**.
After 3 half-lives the net decline is **7/8** of the original, i.e. 7 : 8 of the initial value has been lost.
Always state clearly **what** the ratio compares (remaining : initial, or decline : initial).

callouts.p: Fraction remaining after n half-lives = (1/2)^n. Net decline as a fraction of initial = 1 - (1/2)^n.

core.p: The half-life idea only works well for **large numbers** of nuclei. With just a few nuclei, the randomness is obvious: you might expect half of 4 nuclei to decay in one half-life, but you could easily see 1 or 3 decay instead.
bullets: Half-life is a **statistical** quantity: it describes average behaviour.
For a **single nucleus**, half-life tells you it has a **50% chance** of decaying within one half-life.
Larger samples give results **closer to the prediction** because random variations average out.
This is why repeated count rate readings vary, and why we take **averages over a long time**.

callouts.p: If asked when one nucleus will decay, the answer is that it cannot be predicted because decay is random.

core.p: Random decay can be modelled with **dice, coins or cubes**. Each object represents an unstable nucleus. Each throw represents a fixed time interval. Objects showing a particular face are 'decayed' and removed.
bullets: Start with e.g. **100 dice**; throw them all.
Remove any showing a **six** (each has a 1/6 chance of 'decaying' per throw).
Count and record the number **remaining**, then throw again.
Plot number remaining against number of throws: an **exponential decay curve** appears.
Read off the **half-life in throws** (about 3.8 throws for dice with 1/6 chance).
The model shows that individual decays are **unpredictable** but the overall pattern is predictable.
Limitation: real samples contain **far more nuclei**, so real curves are much smoother.

core.p: When measuring count rate from a short half-life source (such as protactinium-234), you must first measure **background radiation** with no source present, then subtract it from every reading.
bullets: Measure the background count rate over several minutes and find a mean.
Record count rate from the source at regular time intervals.
**Corrected count rate = measured count rate - background count rate**.
Plot corrected count rate against time and find the half-life from the graph.
Keep the distance between source and detector **constant** throughout.
If background is not subtracted, the curve levels off at the background value, and the half-life read off will be **too long**.

callouts.p: Forgetting to subtract background is a classic error in half-life calculations from data tables.

core.p: Knowing the half-life tells you **how long a source stays radioactive** and therefore which isotopes suit which jobs. This links forward to the uses and hazards topic.
bullets: **Short half-life**: activity falls quickly, so the source is safer to use inside the body.
**Long half-life**: the source stays active for a long time, useful for long-term uses but a long-term hazard.
Half-life is used in **radioactive dating** (e.g. carbon-14) to estimate the age of materials.
A high initial activity with a short half-life can still be dangerous at first.

analogy.p: Imagine a pan of corn kernels being heated. You cannot predict which kernel will pop next or exactly when, but with thousands of kernels you can say confidently that about half will have popped in a certain time. That is like random decay and half-life. Where it breaks down: popcorn pops because of heating and the rate depends on temperature, whereas radioactive decay is spontaneous and completely unaffected by temperature or any outside conditions. Also, unpopped kernels get more likely to pop as they heat up, but an undecayed nucleus never becomes more likely to decay with age.

terms.d: A nucleus that will decay by emitting radiation to become more stable.
The random process in which an unstable nucleus emits radiation to become more stable.
Unpredictable for an individual nucleus: you cannot know which nucleus will decay or when.
Happening without any outside cause; decay is unaffected by temperature, pressure or chemical state.
The number of unstable nuclei that decay per second, measured in becquerels (Bq).
The unit of activity; 1 Bq equals one decay per second.
The number of decays recorded per second or per minute by a detector.
A detector that produces a pulse each time ionising radiation enters it, connected to a counter.
The time taken for the number of unstable nuclei in a sample, or its count rate, to halve.
Ionising radiation always present from natural and man-made sources, which must be subtracted from readings.
The measured count rate minus the background count rate.
A decrease in which the quantity falls by the same fraction in equal time intervals, giving a curve that never reaches zero.
The overall decrease in activity or number of nuclei after a time, often expressed as a ratio of the initial value.
The fixed chance that a given nucleus decays in a set time; the same for all nuclei of an isotope.

mistakes.w: Half-life is half the time it takes for the sample to decay completely.
mistakes.r: Half-life is the time for the number of unstable nuclei or count rate to halve.

mistakes.w: Half-life is the time for the mass of the sample to halve.
mistakes.r: It is the number of undecayed nuclei (or activity) that halves; the total mass barely changes since daughter nuclei remain.

mistakes.w: After two half-lives the sample has completely decayed.
mistakes.r: After two half-lives one quarter of the unstable nuclei remain.

mistakes.w: Heating the source speeds up its decay.
mistakes.r: Radioactive decay is random and spontaneous and is not affected by temperature.

mistakes.w: You can predict when a particular nucleus will decay using half-life.
mistakes.r: It is impossible to predict when a particular nucleus will decay; decay is random.

mistakes.w: Using the measured count rates directly to find half-life.
mistakes.r: Subtract background count rate from each reading first.

mistakes.w: After 3 half-lives, 3/8 remains.
mistakes.r: After 3 half-lives (1/2)^3 = 1/8 remains.

mistakes.w: Half-life gets shorter as the sample gets smaller.
mistakes.r: Half-life is constant for an isotope regardless of how much is present.

exam.q: State what is meant by the half-life of a radioactive isotope.
model: Time taken for the number of unstable nuclei / count rate / activity to halve
exam.tip: Mention nuclei or count rate; 'the substance halves' does not score.

exam.q: Explain what is meant by radioactive decay being random.
model: You cannot predict which nucleus will decay
or when a particular nucleus will decay
exam.tip: Two ideas: which and when.

exam.q: A source has a count rate of 640 counts per minute. Its half-life is 3 hours. Calculate the count rate after 12 hours.
model: 12 / 3 = 4 half-lives
640 / 2^4 = 40 counts per minute
exam.tip: Find the number of half-lives first.

exam.q: The activity of a sample falls from 2400 Bq to 300 Bq in 24 days. Calculate its half-life.
model: 2400 to 1200 to 600 to 300 = 3 half-lives
= 8 days
exam.tip: Show the halving chain so method marks are clear.

exam.q: Why must background count be subtracted before calculating half-life?
model: Background radiation is detected as well as radiation from the source
Otherwise readings are too high and half-life found is incorrect (too long)
exam.tip: Say what the error would do.

exam.q: (Higher) Calculate the ratio of final activity to initial activity after 4 half-lives.
exam.tip: Ratio = 1 : 2^n.

exam.q: (Higher) A sample has an initial activity of 8000 Bq. Calculate the net decline in activity after 3 half-lives, and express it as a fraction of the initial activity.
model: Remaining = 8000 / 8 = 1000 Bq
Net decline = 8000 - 1000 = 7000 Bq
As fraction of initial = 7/8
exam.tip: Decline is the drop, not what remains.

exam.q: A student has 4 atoms of an isotope. Explain why exactly 2 may not have decayed after one half-life.
model: Decay is random
Half-life is a statistical average that only applies reliably to large numbers of nuclei
exam.tip: Link small numbers to randomness.

exam.q: Describe how you would use 100 dice to model radioactive decay and find a 'half-life'.
model: Throw all dice; each die represents an unstable nucleus
Remove dice showing a chosen number (e.g. a six) as decayed
Count and record remaining dice, repeat for many throws
Plot number remaining against throw number and read time for number to halve
exam.tip: Say what each part of the model represents.

exam.q: A student measures the count rate of a radioactive source over 10 minutes. Describe how she should plan and analyse the experiment to obtain an accurate value of half-life, and explain why decay is described as random.
model: Measure background count rate (no source) over a long time and find the mean
Measure count rate of source at regular time intervals, keeping distance constant
Subtract background from each reading to get corrected count rate
Plot corrected count rate against time and draw a smooth curve
Read off time for count rate to halve from several starting points and average
Readings fluctuate because decay is random: cannot predict which nucleus decays or when
exam.tip: A strong answer has method, analysis and explanation linked together.

worked.q: Iodine-131 has a half-life of 8 days. A hospital receives a sample with activity 3200 Bq. What is its activity after 32 days?
steps: Number of half-lives = 32 / 8 = 4.
Activity after 4 half-lives = 3200 x (1/2)^4.

worked.q: A table shows corrected count rates of 960, 480, 240 and 120 counts/min at 0, 15, 30 and 45 minutes. Find the half-life and the fraction of nuclei remaining after 60 minutes.
steps: 960 to 480 takes 15 minutes, 480 to 240 takes 15 minutes: half-life = 15 minutes.
60 minutes / 15 minutes = 4 half-lives.
Fraction remaining = (1/2)^4 = 1/16.
Count rate at 60 minutes = 960 / 16 = 60 counts/min.
worked.ans: Half-life = 15 minutes; 1/16 of the nuclei remain after 60 minutes (60 counts/min).

worked.q: (Higher) A source has measured count rate 530 counts/min, with background 30 counts/min. Its half-life is 2 hours. Find the measured count rate after 6 hours and the net decline as a ratio of the initial corrected count rate.
steps: Corrected initial count rate = 530 - 30 = 500 counts/min.
6 / 2 = 3 half-lives; corrected count rate after = 500 / 8 = 62.5 counts/min.
Measured count rate after = 62.5 + 30 = 92.5 counts/min (about 93).
Net decline = 500 - 62.5 = 437.5 counts/min; as a ratio of initial = 437.5 : 500 = 7 : 8.
worked.ans: About 93 counts/min measured; net decline is 7/8 of the initial corrected count rate (ratio 7 : 8).

phy_ocra.14.4.summary: Alpha, beta and gamma radiation have very different **penetrating powers** because they differ in mass, charge and how strongly they ionise. **Alpha** is stopped by a sheet of paper or a few centimetres of air, **beta** by a few millimetres of aluminium, and **gamma** is only reduced by thick lead or several metres of concrete. The more strongly a radiation **ionises**, the faster it loses energy and the **less penetrating** it is, which explains both the absorption results and how each type is used and handled safely.

core.h: The three types of nuclear radiation
core.p: Unstable nuclei emit **alpha particles**, **beta particles** or **gamma rays**. Each has a different nature, and this decides how far it can travel through materials before being absorbed.
bullets: **Alpha particle**: 2 protons + 2 neutrons (a helium nucleus); charge **+2**; relatively heavy (relative mass 4).
**Beta particle**: a **fast-moving electron** emitted from the nucleus when a neutron changes into a proton; charge **-1**; very small mass.
**Gamma ray**: **electromagnetic radiation** of very high frequency; **no charge** and **no mass**.
All three are **ionising radiation**: they can knock electrons out of atoms they pass.

callouts.p: Alpha: stopped by paper. Beta: stopped by a few mm of aluminium. Gamma: reduced (not completely stopped) by several cm of lead or metres of concrete.

core.p: **Penetrating power** describes how far a type of radiation can travel through a material before being **absorbed**. Radiation is absorbed when it has transferred all of its energy to the material, mainly by ionising atoms along its path.
bullets: Low penetration = **absorbed quickly**, in a short distance.
High penetration = travels a **long way** through materials before being absorbed.
Penetration depends on both the **type of radiation** and the **material** (denser materials such as lead absorb more).
Thicker absorbers absorb more radiation, so **count rate falls as thickness increases**.

callouts.p: How far a type of radiation can pass through a material before it is absorbed.

core.h: Why alpha is the least penetrating
core.p: Alpha particles are **large, heavy and have a +2 charge**. As they pass through matter they interact very strongly with atoms, pulling electrons away and **ionising** many atoms in a very short distance. Each ionisation uses up some of the particle's energy, so it **runs out of energy quickly**.
bullets: **Most strongly ionising** of the three types.
Produces **thousands of ion pairs per mm** of air.
Range in air of only **a few centimetres** (around 3 to 7 cm).
Stopped by a **sheet of paper**, the **outer dead layer of skin**, or clothing.
Outside the body alpha is **low risk** because it cannot reach living cells, but inside the body it is **the most dangerous** because all of its ionisation happens in a small region of living tissue.

callouts.p: The more strongly ionising a radiation is, the less penetrating it is, because it loses its energy over a shorter distance.

core.p: Beta particles are **fast electrons**, much smaller than alpha particles and with only a **-1 charge**. They interact less strongly with atoms, so they ionise less per millimetre and can travel further before losing all their energy.
bullets: **Moderately ionising**: weaker than alpha, stronger than gamma.
Range in air of **up to about 1 metre**.
Passes through paper but is **stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium** (about 3 to 5 mm).
Can pass through skin and reach living tissue, so is a hazard **outside and inside** the body.
Used in **thickness gauges** for paper, card and thin sheet materials, because small changes in thickness cause measurable changes in count rate.

core.h: Why gamma is the most penetrating
core.p: Gamma rays are **electromagnetic waves** with **no charge and no mass**. They interact only weakly with atoms, so they cause **few ionisations** per unit length and keep their energy over long distances.
bullets: **Least ionising** of the three.
Range in air is **very large**; intensity decreases mainly because the rays **spread out**.
Passes easily through paper and aluminium.
Intensity is **reduced** by several centimetres of **lead** or several metres of **concrete**, but is **never completely stopped**.
Dangerous from **outside** the body because it can reach internal organs.
Used for **sterilising** medical equipment and food, as **tracers**, and in radiotherapy, because it passes through containers and the body.

callouts.p: Write that lead REDUCES or ABSORBS MOST gamma radiation. Saying gamma is completely stopped by lead can lose marks.

core.p: The key idea connecting everything in this point is that **ionisation uses up energy**. A particle that ionises many atoms per millimetre spends its energy fast, so it cannot penetrate far.
bullets: Alpha: **high ionisation**, **low penetration**.
Beta: **medium ionisation**, **medium penetration**.
Gamma: **low ionisation**, **high penetration**.
Bigger charge and bigger mass mean **stronger interactions** with electrons in atoms.

core.p: You can identify the type(s) of radiation from a source by placing different absorbers between the source and a **Geiger-Muller (GM) tube** and recording the count rate. This is often done as a teacher demonstration because of the hazard.
bullets: Measure **background count rate** first with no source present.
Measure count rate with **no absorber**, then with **paper**, then **a few mm aluminium**, then **thick lead**.
Keep the **distance** between source and detector **constant** (and short, a few cm, so alpha can reach the tube).
Subtract background from every reading to get the **corrected count rate**.
A big drop when **paper** is added means the source emits **alpha**.
A big drop when **aluminium** is added means **beta** is present.
A count well above background that remains after aluminium and is only reduced by lead means **gamma** is present.
