core.p: Even air absorbs radiation, because it contains atoms that can be ionised. Measuring count rate as the detector is moved away from a source shows the **range in air**.
bullets: Alpha count rate drops to background at about **5 cm** from the source.
Beta can be detected up to around **1 m** away.
Gamma count rate falls with distance mostly because it **spreads out**, not because air absorbs much.
Increasing **distance** from a source is one of the simplest ways to **reduce exposure**.

core.h: Penetration and hazards to the body
core.p: How dangerous a source is depends on whether it is **outside or inside** the body, which links directly to penetrating power.
bullets: **Outside the body**: gamma and beta are most dangerous because they can **penetrate skin** and reach organs; alpha is stopped by the dead outer skin layer.
**Inside the body** (swallowed or breathed in): alpha is most dangerous, because it is **strongly ionising** and all of its energy is absorbed by nearby cells.
Inside the body gamma is the **least dangerous**, because most of it passes out of the body without ionising.
Ionisation can **damage or kill cells** and damage **DNA**, which may lead to mutations and cancer.

callouts.p: Never say alpha is always the most dangerous. State whether the source is inside or outside the body and explain using ionising and penetrating power.

core.p: Penetrating power decides which type of source is suitable for a use. Exam questions often ask you to justify a choice.
bullets: **Smoke detectors** use **alpha**: it ionises air strongly and is absorbed by smoke, but cannot escape the detector casing.
**Paper thickness gauges** use **beta**: it is partly absorbed by paper, so count rate changes with thickness; alpha would be fully stopped and gamma would pass straight through.
**Medical tracers** usually use **gamma**: it penetrates the body to reach a detector outside, and is weakly ionising so causes less harm.
**Sterilisation** uses **gamma**: it penetrates packaging to kill microbes inside.
**Shielding**: lead aprons, lead-lined containers and thick concrete are used where gamma is present.

callouts.p: For a gauge question, explain why the other two radiations would not work, not just why the chosen one does.

core.p: Because all three types are ionising, sources are handled to limit exposure. The precautions use ideas of penetration and distance.
bullets: Use **tongs** to keep sources at arm's length (increase distance).
Store sources in **lead-lined boxes** to absorb radiation.
Never point sources at people; **minimise time** of exposure.
Workers wear **dosimeter badges** to monitor exposure.

analogy.p: Imagine rolling objects through a crowded room. A heavy bowling ball (alpha) crashes into lots of people straight away, knocking them over (ionising), and quickly comes to a stop. A small marble (beta) bumps into fewer people and gets further. A ghost (gamma) passes through almost everyone without touching them, so it travels right across the room and only rarely knocks anyone over. Where it breaks down: alpha and beta are slowed by electrical forces from charge, not physical collisions, and gamma is a wave of energy, not an object; it is absorbed gradually by dense materials such as lead rather than passing through everything.

terms.d: A particle of 2 protons and 2 neutrons (helium nucleus) emitted from an unstable nucleus; charge +2.
A fast-moving electron emitted from the nucleus when a neutron turns into a proton; charge -1.
High-frequency electromagnetic radiation emitted from an unstable nucleus; no charge and no mass.
Radiation with enough energy to remove electrons from atoms, producing ions.
How strongly a radiation ionises the atoms it passes, i.e. how many ions it produces per unit distance.
How far a radiation can travel through a material before being absorbed.
The transfer of the radiation's energy to a material so that the radiation no longer passes through.
A material such as paper, aluminium or lead placed in the path of radiation to absorb it.
The distance a radiation can travel in a material such as air before it is completely absorbed.
A detector of ionising radiation; each particle or ray entering it produces a pulse that is counted.
The number of counts per second or per minute recorded by a detector.
Low-level ionising radiation always present from natural and man-made sources.
Measured count rate minus background count rate.
Material placed around a source to absorb radiation and protect people, e.g. lead or concrete.
An atom that has gained or lost electrons and so has an overall charge.

mistakes.w: Gamma rays are stopped completely by lead.
mistakes.r: Gamma is reduced (most is absorbed) by several cm of lead; it is never completely stopped.

mistakes.w: Alpha is the most penetrating because it is the biggest.
mistakes.r: Alpha is the least penetrating; its large mass and charge make it strongly ionising so it loses energy quickly.

mistakes.w: Beta is stopped by paper.
mistakes.r: Beta passes through paper and is stopped by a few mm of aluminium.

mistakes.w: Gamma is the most ionising.
mistakes.r: Gamma is the least ionising and the most penetrating.

mistakes.w: Alpha is always the most dangerous radiation.
mistakes.r: Alpha is most dangerous inside the body; outside, gamma and beta are more hazardous because they penetrate skin.

mistakes.w: Count rate fell after paper so the source emits beta.
mistakes.r: A fall when paper is added shows alpha; beta is identified by a fall when aluminium is added.

mistakes.w: Use gamma for a paper thickness gauge.
mistakes.r: Beta is used: gamma would pass straight through paper with almost no change in count rate.

mistakes.w: Forgetting background when deciding if any radiation passes through lead.
mistakes.r: Compare with background: if the count after lead equals background, no gamma is getting through.

exam.q: Name the type of radiation that is stopped by a sheet of paper.
model: Alpha
exam.tip: Paper = alpha; aluminium = beta; lead = gamma.

exam.q: State what is needed to absorb most beta radiation.
model: A few mm of aluminium
exam.tip: Give a thickness: 'a few millimetres'.

exam.q: Put alpha, beta and gamma radiation in order of increasing penetrating power.
model: Alpha, beta, gamma
exam.tip: Increasing = least first.

exam.q: Explain why alpha particles have a short range in air.
model: Alpha particles are strongly ionising
so they lose their energy quickly / over a short distance
exam.tip: Link ionising to energy loss.

exam.q: Explain why gamma radiation is used to sterilise surgical instruments sealed in plastic packs.
model: Gamma is highly penetrating so passes through the packaging
and kills bacteria/microorganisms on the instruments
exam.tip: Two parts: why it gets there, what it does.

exam.q: A source gives corrected count rates: no absorber 400 counts/min, paper 400 counts/min, 3 mm aluminium 120 counts/min, 2 cm lead 10 counts/min. State which radiations the source emits and explain.
model: No alpha: no drop with paper
Beta present: large drop with aluminium
Gamma present: count still above zero after aluminium, reduced by lead
exam.tip: Use each pair of readings in turn.

exam.q: Explain why beta radiation, not alpha or gamma, is used to monitor the thickness of paper in a factory.
model: Beta is partly absorbed by paper so count rate changes with thickness
Alpha would be completely absorbed by the paper
Gamma would pass straight through with almost no change in count rate
exam.tip: Eliminate the other two.

exam.q: Explain why an alpha source is more dangerous inside the body than outside.
model: Outside, alpha is stopped by the skin / dead skin layer
Inside, it is strongly ionising and damages nearby cells/DNA
exam.tip: Use both inside and outside ideas.

exam.q: Describe how a student could use a Geiger-Muller tube and absorbers to find which types of radiation are emitted by a source.
model: Measure background count rate first
Measure count rate with no absorber, then paper, then aluminium, then lead, at a fixed distance
Subtract background from each reading
Drop with paper = alpha; drop with aluminium = beta; count remaining after aluminium reduced by lead = gamma
exam.tip: Mention constant distance and background correction for full marks.

exam.q: Compare alpha, beta and gamma radiation in terms of their nature, ionising power and penetrating power, and explain the link between ionising and penetrating power.
model: Alpha: helium nucleus, +2 charge, strongly ionising, stopped by paper / few cm air
Beta: fast electron, -1 charge, moderately ionising, stopped by few mm aluminium
Gamma: EM wave, no charge or mass, weakly ionising, reduced by thick lead/concrete
Ionisation transfers energy from the radiation to atoms
Strongly ionising radiation loses energy over a short distance so is less penetrating
Larger charge/mass means stronger interaction with atoms, so more ionisation
exam.tip: Structure as a comparison, then give the linking explanation.

worked.q: Background count is 25 counts/min. A source gives: no absorber 865, paper 445, 4 mm aluminium 445, 5 cm lead 25 counts/min. Identify the radiations emitted.
steps: Corrected readings: 840, 420, 420, 0 counts/min.
Paper causes a fall from 840 to 420: alpha is present.
Aluminium causes no further fall: no beta.
Count remains at 420 after aluminium and falls to background with lead: gamma present.
worked.ans: The source emits alpha and gamma radiation, but no beta.

worked.q: Model answer: A hospital needs a radioactive tracer injected into a patient and detected by a camera outside the body. Explain why a gamma emitter is chosen.
steps: The radiation must travel from inside the body to the camera outside.
Alpha would be absorbed within the body and not detected; it is also very ionising, so would damage cells.
Beta would be largely absorbed by tissue and also ionise cells.
Gamma is highly penetrating so it leaves the body, and is weakly ionising so causes the least harm.
worked.ans: Gamma penetrates the body to reach the detector and is the least ionising, so it can be detected while minimising cell damage.

worked.q: Applied example: A paper mill uses a beta source above the paper and a detector below. The count rate rises. What has happened and how should the rollers respond?
steps: A higher count rate means less beta is being absorbed.
Less absorption means the paper has become thinner.
The rollers should move apart (reduce the pressure) to make the paper thicker again.
worked.ans: The paper is too thin; the rollers apply less pressure until the count rate returns to the set value.
